new_statements.quote: Buakaw et al. 2018 p.5: "The sesquisyllable consists of one main syllable preceded by a presyllable. Phonologically, presyllable is an unstressed syllable the vowel of which is limited to low central vowel /a/"; p.6: "The minor syllable of Katiang is an unstressed syllable, namely a presyllable ... The vowel /a/ in a presyllable is pronounced as a schwa [ə]." || Chen, Wang & Lai 1986 p.18: "一般音节中的元音是固定的，清晰的，不是轻读的，而前加音节中的元音，始终是以轻读、弱化形式出现，含糊不清，很不稳定。" || Dai & Liu 1997 p.93 (Guangka Rumai): "Guangka has a 31 tone. This tone only appears in the first (weakened) syllable of polysyllabic words ... When the weakened syllable of a polysyllabic word serves as a prefix, the tone is not clear"
new_statements.translation: Chen et al. 1986 p.18: 'The vowel of an ordinary (main) syllable is fixed and clear and is not read lightly [unstressed], whereas the vowel of a presyllable always appears in a light, weakened form, indistinct and very unstable.'
new_statements.citation: Buakaw, Supakit, Ampika Rattanapitak & Sujaritlak Deepadung. 2018. Katiang Palaung of Hsipaw: Phonology and classification. Dialectologia 21: 1-16. [cross-checked with Chen Xiangmu, Wang Jingliu & Lai Yongliang. 1986. De'angyu jianzhi. Beijing: Minzu chubanshe, p.18; and Dai Qingxia & Liu Yan. 1997. Analysis of the tones in the Guangka subdialect of De'ang. Mon-Khmer Studies 27: 91-108, pp.92-93]
new_statements.locator: Buakaw et al. 2018: p.5 sec. 2.1.2 'Polysyllabic words' and p.6 sec. 2.2 (minor syllable). Chen et al. 1986: p.18 (sec. 二 音节结构, 2. 前加音节, note (2)). Dai & Liu 1997: p.92 (sec. 1) and p.93.
new_statements.translation_language: English (Buakaw 2018; Dai & Liu 1997 in Evans's translation) and Chinese (Chen et al. 1986)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables (presyllable + major syllable). Stress falls on the major syllable, which is the final syllable of the word; the presyllable is unstressed, its vowel reduced to schwa (Katiang) or 'light/weakened, indistinct, unstable' (Bulei). In Rumai proper (Guangka, Ruili) the major syllable carries one of three fixed lexical tones while the weakened first syllable has no clear tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. Compound words (two major syllables) are not assigned a stress pattern by any source. Dai & Liu 1997: in Guangka the tone of the first syllable of a disyllable varies with the tone of the second; some words lack a fixed tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms: the sesquisyllabic word = (presyllable) + major syllable; only the major (final) syllable is stressed. The three sources cover three different varieties filed under rbb/ruma1248: Buakaw et al. 2018 = Katiang of Hsipaw (non-tonal description); Chen et al. 1986 p.18 = Yunqian/Bulei, Luxi (no lexical tone, p.16); Dai & Liu 1997 = Guangka, Ruili = Rumai proper, which is TONAL (three fixed tones; the presyllable is 'weakened' and its tone unclear; p.93) and Chen et al. 1986 p.108 also gives the Rumai dialect two tones (55, 51). If the catalog wants the Rumai-proper variety, the reading would be tonal-with-stress-statement with the same major-syllable prominence; the Katiang/Bulei statements are the only ones that use the word stress/轻读.
new_statements.identity_note: ruma1248 / ISO rbb lumps several varieties. The deciding English statement (Buakaw et al. 2018, Glottolog phonology ref for ruma1248) describes Katiang of Hsipaw, which its authors place between the Dehong Palaung group (Liang, Pule, Rumai) and the Darang group, 'closer to Darang' — not Rumai of Namhkam proper. Chen, Wang & Lai 1986 p.18 describes the Yunqian/Bulei 布雷 dialect (Luxi, Yunnan), which Glottolog 2015 group with Pule/Pale [pce]; its Rumai 汝买 dialect sketch (p.108) and Dai & Liu 1997 (Guangka, Ruili) describe Rumai proper in China, which is tonal (2-3 tones). Rumai of Nam Hkam/Man Ton (Myanmar, Weymuth's variety, the bulk of speakers) has no accessible phonological description yet (Weymuth 2022 not opened).

sources.note: Bibliography only; annotates Chen/Wang/Lai 1986 (Chinese), Dai & Liu 1997 ('Guangka is a subdialect of the Rumai dialect'), Janzen 1978 (Pale vs Gold- and Rumai-Palaung, unpublished Mysore paper), Newlands 1994 Rumai wordlist (ms.), Yan Qixiang 1983 (Minzu Yuwen).

sources.citation: Dai Qingxia & Liu Yan. 1997. Analysis of the tones in the Guangka subdialect of De'ang (transl. Jonathan Evans). Mon-Khmer Studies 27: 91-108. SEAlang SALA archive scan.
sources.note: Rumai proper (Guangka village, Mengxiu, Ruili). p.92: 'Guangka has three tones; almost every syllable has a fixed tone, and there are many tonal minimal pairs.' p.93: 'Guangka has a 31 tone. This tone only appears in the first (weakened) syllable of polysyllabic words, and in borrowings from Chinese. When the weakened syllable of a polysyllabic word serves as a prefix, the tone is not clear.' p.99: Chayeqing (Rumai) has high level and high falling tones; Yunqian (Bulei) and Xiaochanggou (Liang) have no tones. The word 'stress' is never used.

sources.citation: Chen Xiangmu 陈相木, Wang Jingliu 王敬骝 & Lai Yongliang 赖永良. 1986. De'angyu jianzhi 德昂语简志. Beijing: Minzu chubanshe. Archive.org community scan (item 20220317_20220317_1057) with scanned text layer.
sources.note: Base variety Yunqian 允欠, Luxi = Bulei dialect (pp.4-5). p.18: '一般音节中的元音是固定的，清晰的，不是轻读的，而前加音节中的元音，始终是以轻读、弱化形式出现，含糊不清，很不稳定。' (main-syllable vowel fixed/clear/not light; presyllable vowel always light and weakened). p.7: presyllables k, t, s 'carry a weakened vowel'. p.16: Bulei 'has no tones (字调)'; short-vowel syllables read high-falling, long-vowel lower-falling in slow speech. p.101: dialects Bulei / Rumai 汝买 (Longchuan, Ruili) / Liang. p.108 (Rumai dialect sketch): '汝买话不仅有元音长短的区别，而且还有声调的区分…只分高平调〔55〕和全降调〔51〕两个调' (Rumai has two tones). No 重音 (stress) statement anywhere.
